title: Post-Course Portfolio: Real-Time Chat Application
descriptionMarkdown:
# Real-Time Chat Application

## Position in the curriculum

Post-course portfolio: build after the Real-Time Tic-Tac-Toe project (for the WebSocket foundation) and the Authentication & User Management System (for real login), since this project combines both rather than introducing either from scratch.

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`chat-room-ledger-checkpoint`** ("Room-scoped message ledger"), a pure in-memory `ChatLedger.run(String input)` program implementing exactly the room-membership, message-ordering, and history-query core. Passing its hidden tests proves your ledger's ordering and scoping rules are correct, independent of any real WebSocket transport or database.

The real-time delivery over a WebSocket connection and authenticating that connection itself are external and self-reviewed.

## Beyond what the lessons taught

This project assumes the WebSocket research already done for the game projects. Authenticating a WebSocket connection itself (rather than a plain HTTP request) is a specific detail Spring Security's documentation covers but the course's Chapter 23 authentication material does not — research it deliberately as part of this project.

## Architecture overview

```text
ChatWebSocketHandler            <- authenticates the handshake, routes JOIN/SEND messages
ChatService                      <- your checkpoint's membership/ordering rules, reshaped as a Spring bean
Room / Message (JPA entities)     <- Message carries a global sequence id, room, user, text, persisted immediately
ChatHistoryController             <- GET /api/rooms/{id}/messages, ordinary paginated REST, not WebSocket
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into a service.** Carry your join/leave/send/history rules into `ChatService`, unit tests unchanged, backed by a real `Message` entity instead of an in-memory list.
2. **Slice 2 — persist before broadcast.** Wire `SEND` so the message is durably written to the database before (or atomically with) being broadcast to connected room members; test what happens to history if a broadcast step were to fail.
3. **Slice 3 — authenticate the WebSocket handshake.** Reject an unauthenticated connection attempt before any message can be sent or received; research Spring Security's WebSocket handshake interceptor for this.
4. **Slice 4 — the REST history endpoint.** Paginated `GET /api/rooms/{id}/messages`, stably ordered, so a client that just joined can catch up without replaying the WebSocket stream from the beginning.
5. **Slice 5 — presence.** Track and broadcast who is currently connected to a room, updated on connect/disconnect.

## Common pitfalls

- **Broadcasting a message before it is durably persisted.** A server restart between broadcast and persistence must never lose a message from history; persist first, exactly as the checkpoint's own `SEND` always records before reporting success.
- **Authenticating the initial HTTP upgrade request but never re-checking identity for the WebSocket session itself.** Bind the authenticated identity to the WebSocket session at handshake time, not per-message.
- **Broadcasting every room's messages to every connected client.** Scope a broadcast strictly to clients connected to the specific room a message was sent to, exactly as the checkpoint's own `HISTORY` is scoped per room.
- **Using an unstable or per-room-reset id for pagination.** The checkpoint's single global sequence (shared across every room) is deliberately the model to follow, so ordering stays stable even as history grows.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Attempt a WebSocket connection with no authentication at all and confirm it is refused at the handshake, before any message exchange.
- Send several messages, then kill and restart the server process, and confirm every message is still present via the REST history endpoint.
- Connect a client to room A only and confirm it never receives a broadcast for a message sent to room B.

## Required evidence

- A persistence test confirming every sent message is durably stored before (or atomically with) being broadcast, so a server restart between send and broadcast does not lose the message from history.
- An authentication test confirming an unauthenticated WebSocket handshake is rejected before any message exchange is possible.
- A pagination test for the REST history endpoint, confirming stable chronological ordering across pages.
- A test confirming a message sent to room A is never broadcast to a client connected only to room B.
- A presence test confirming a disconnect is detected and reflected to remaining room members within a reasonable, documented time bound.

## Review and completion

A reviewer joins a room, sends several messages, disconnects, reconnects, and confirms the full message history (including messages sent while disconnected, sent by other users) is available via the REST endpoint — then attempts to connect to the WebSocket endpoint with no authentication at all and expects the connection to be refused outright.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded room-scoped message ledger checkpoint and carry its verified ordering rules into a real, persisted WebSocket chat service
Persist every message durably before or atomically with broadcasting it, never relying on in-memory state alone
Authenticate a WebSocket handshake itself, not just the HTTP requests around it
Combine a REST endpoint (paginated history) with a WebSocket endpoint (live updates) for the same underlying data
Scope a broadcast correctly to only the clients connected to the relevant room
